sections.title: Exam predictions
sections.tally: 27 questions · from the complete study guide
sections.note:
The reason to read this section

Five things appear in the predictions that the revision paper never asks for. If the real paper draws from the same syllabus, these are your blind spots:

  • Warshall / Floyd-Warshall applied numerically. The revision paper only asks you to compare it with Dijkstra (Q15). Here you must run an iteration and produce the matrix.
  • Bellman-Ford on actual negative weights. Again, comparison only in Q15; here you compute distances that go negative.
  • Boolean algebra and De Morgan simplification. The paper does K-maps and NAND universality (Q27); it never asks you to simplify an expression by naming each law.
  • PERT forward pass with ES and EF from a predecessor table. Paper Q13 gives you the network already drawn; here you build it from predecessors and compute earliest start and finish.
  • Lattice and Boolean algebra as definitions. Paper Q24 works the divisors of 12; here you must define a lattice and a Boolean algebra in the abstract.

sections.title: Two more papers: Data Communications and Computer Networks
sections.note:
What these are, and how much to trust them

The lecture note you uploaded ends with two examination papers in the same subject: a regular examination sat in November 2024 and a model paper. They are not papers and they are not set by your department, so they carry much less weight than CSC427. Their format is different too: 3 hours, 60 marks, ten one mark questions in Part A and then five sections of 10 marks, one question chosen from each.

Use them for coverage, not for style. Two things make them worth the half hour. Part A is twenty rapid fire definitions, which is exactly the recall the CSC427 paper rewarded and exactly the kind of thing that is either instant or lost. And Part B reaches for topics no other paper on this page touches: sliding window protocols, polling, CIDR, the transition to IPv6, TCP timer management, the architecture of e-mail. If you can answer these, no reasonable question on your paper will be unfamiliar.

sections.title: Mock exam: everything CSC427 did not ask
sections.note:
What this is and why it is shaped this way

The CSC427 paper above is the only real evidence we have of how this department words a data communications exam. It is worth reading twice for its style: three parts per question, lettered a, b, c, each part carrying sub-parts, heavy on "define, list, discuss, distinguish", and it asks for diagrams by name.

But notice what that paper never touched: not one calculation. No channel capacity, no CRC, no Hamming code, no subnetting, no multiplexing arithmetic. Those topics are core to this course and they are the ones an examiner reaches for when a paper needs to separate a 70 from a 50. This mock is written in the CSC427 house style but aimed squarely at the half of the syllabus that paper left alone, so between the two you have the course covered.

E → E + T | E - T | T
T → T * F | T / F | F
F → ( E ) | id
id → A | B | C | D

This is the classic expression grammar: it builds in the fact that * and / bind tighter than + and -, and that operators are left-associative. Every parse tree below follows from it.
